analysis.one_liner: Requires employers, government agencies, and businesses to make their websites and apps usable by people with disabilities.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being referred to two House committees in May 2025, no further action has been taken on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would tell the Justice Department and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission to write clear, uniform rules requiring that websites and apps used for jobs, government services, business services, and testing be accessible to people with disabilities — including online-only businesses. It would let individuals and the government sue over inaccessible sites, seek damages and civil penalties, and it would set up a technical assistance center and grants of up to $10,000 to help small businesses comply. It has not advanced past committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: About one in four U.S. adults lives with a disability; for those who are blind, deaf, or have other disabilities, the bill would mean websites and apps for jobs, government services, shopping, banking, and testing must work with screen readers, captions, and other assistive technology, with the same ease of use as everyone else [S2]. Small businesses that must comply also benefit from grants of up to $10,000 to help them fix inaccessible content, and from longer compliance deadlines [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It directs the Justice Department and the EEOC to write binding federal standards making websites and apps used by employers, government, businesses, and test providers usable by people with disabilities, with the same ease of use as everyone else.

It clarifies that the ADA covers all websites and apps of public accommodations — including online-only businesses — closing a gap some courts created by reading the ADA as limited to physical places.

It lets individuals with disabilities sue directly in state or federal court without exhausting administrative remedies, lets the Attorney General seek civil penalties and compensatory and punitive damages on their behalf, and awards attorney's fees to prevailing plaintiffs.
It gives small businesses extra lead time (3 years for public-accommodation rules, 2 for employment rules) and grants of up to $10,000 to help small entities audit and fix inaccessible content.

It creates a standing advisory committee a majority of whose members have disabilities, requires public posting of enforcement settlements, and mandates a study of how emerging technologies affect people with disabilities.

analysis.who_pays: Covered entities — employers, public agencies, public accommodations, testing companies — and the web developers and commercial providers that build their sites, who would have to audit and remediate their web content and applications to meet the new standards; the Justice Department and EEOC also gain substantial new enforcement work, funded by authorized spending of $35.15 million per year for fiscal years 2026–2035 [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Businesses and public agencies with inaccessible sites

drawbacks.text: Compliance would cost money: nearly every business and government office with a website would have to audit, redesign, and test it to meet federal standards, and large entities would have to comply just 30 days after the final rule takes effect.

The bill creates a private right of action allowing individuals and classes to sue in court for damages and attorney's fees without first notifying or exhausting remedies with the entity — the bill expressly forbids regulators from requiring advance notice before a lawsuit [S2]. Businesses argue this invites litigation before they get a chance to fix a problem.
It authorizes $35.15 million per year for ten fiscal years (2026–2035) in federal spending for enforcement, technical assistance, and small-business grants.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real: today there is no single enforceable accessibility standard for the web, and people with disabilities routinely cannot complete basic tasks online. The costs fall on businesses that must redesign sites and apps, but the bill phases rules in, explicitly weighs small firms' capabilities, offers up to $10,000 grants to small entities, and retains an "undue burden" defense. The private right of action with damages and fees could spur defensive litigation, and no advance notice of a violation would be required before suing — a fair objection the bill chose not to accommodate. On balance the design is careful and the public benefit is large.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, where nothing has happened since, so no vote has ever been taken on it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 14, 2025 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
The action history shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral.
It attracted 11 cosponsors: 7 of 217 House Democrats and 4 of 223 House Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses with inaccessible websites and apps avoid any new obligation to fix them; people with disabilities continue to face the barriers the bill described.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Inaccessible websites and apps; their owners

for.name: Rep. Steny Hoyer
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: 11 House cosponsors (7 of 217 Democrats, 4 of 223 Republicans)

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor (Republican) and lead cosponsor (Democrat) crossed party lines, and the 11 cosponsors split 7 Democratic and 4 Republican; no opposition ever went on the record because the bill never received a vote.

industries.industry: Web developers and commercial technology providers
industries.note: For the first time they would be directly liable for building or selling inaccessible sites and apps for covered clients, making accessibility a mandatory feature rather than an optional one.

industries.industry: E-commerce, banking, hospitality, and other consumer-facing businesses
industries.note: They would bear the cost of auditing and redesigning websites and apps; they currently externalize the cost onto disabled users who cannot use their services.

industries.industry: ADA litigation and accessibility consulting industry
industries.note: The private right of action, damages, attorney's fees, and mandated audits would create steady paid demand for accessibility consultants, auditors, and plaintiff attorneys — work that is precisely what makes sites usable for disabled users.

analysis.trajectory: With only 11 cosponsors, no committee activity in either chamber, and no sign of a markup, the bill is likely to die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless disability advocates push for a hearing or it is attached to a larger package.
